prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- An audio message reportedly from al Qaeda's deputy chief vows revenge for Israel's air and ground assault on Gaza and calls the Jewish state's actions against Hamas militants "a gift" from U.S. President-elect Barack Obama. Al Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri is said to address Muslims in Gaza in an audio message released Tuesday. The speaker, identified as Ayman al-Zawahiri, addresses Muslims in Gaza. He said the violence "is one part of a series of a crusade war against Islam and these air strikes are a gift from Obama before he takes office, and (Egyptian President) Hosni Mubarak, that traitor, is the main partner in your siege and killing." The message, posted Tuesday on various Islamist Web sites with a picture of al-Zawahiri next to an image of a wounded child, urges militants to rally against Israel. "My Muslim brothers and mujahedeens in Gaza and all over Palestine, with the help of God we are with you in the battle, we will direct our strikes against the crusader Jewish coalition wherever we can." The 10-minute message also address Muslims worldwide, claiming that Obama was portrayed as "the savior who will come and change American policy" during the U.S. election but is now "killing your brothers and sisters in Gaza without mercy or even pity." Obama's transition team did not immediately respond to the message. Earlier Tuesday, the president-elect said he was "deeply concerned" about the loss of life in Gaza and Israel, and he promised to make the issue a top priority in his administration. It was Obama's first public reaction to the ongoing fighting between Israel and Hamas militants in Gaza, which began with Israeli air strikes 11 days ago. He reiterated that only one president can speak for the United States at a time. "Starting at the beginning of our administration, we are going to engage effectively and consistently to try to resolve the conflicts that exist in the Middle East," Obama said. CNN Senior International Correspondent Nic Robertson said the al Qaeda message speaks to al-Zawahiri's cause in two ways: It bashes the new U.S. president before he takes office and it criticizes Mubarak, who has drawn al-Zawahiri's ire for not allowing goods and aid through Egypt's border with Gaza. Al-Zawahiri is a native of Egypt who has served jail time there. Robertson, who is reporting from the Israeli-Gaza border, noted on CNN's "Situation Room" that al-Zawahiri got the message out quickly -- "within 12 days, that's very fast." He said that indicated "there's many issues there that are dear to him."

(CNN) — A recording said to feature al Qaeda’s second-in-command promises retaliation for Israel’s aerial and ground offensive in Gaza. It also describes Israel’s campaign against Hamas militants as “a gift” from U.S. President-elect Barack Obama.

In the audio statement released Tuesday, the person identified as Ayman al-Zawahiri speaks directly to Muslims in Gaza. He characterizes the bloodshed as “one part of a series of a crusade war against Islam,” adding that the airstrikes are “a gift from Obama before he takes office.” He also accuses Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak of being a traitor and “the main partner in your siege and killing.”

The 10-minute recording appeared Tuesday on several Islamist websites, accompanied by a photograph of al-Zawahiri beside an image of an injured child. In it, the speaker calls on militants to unite against Israel.

“My Muslim brothers and mujahedeens in Gaza and all over Palestine, with the help of God we are with you in the battle,” he says. “We will direct our strikes against the crusader Jewish coalition wherever we can.”

The message also appeals to Muslims around the world. It says Obama was presented during the U.S. presidential campaign as “the savior who will come and change American policy,” but claims he is now “killing your brothers and sisters in Gaza without mercy or even pity.”

Obama’s transition team did not immediately issue a response to the recording.

Earlier Tuesday, Obama expressed his first public reaction to the continuing conflict between Israel and Hamas militants in Gaza, which began with Israeli airstrikes 11 days earlier. He said he was “deeply concerned” by the deaths in both Gaza and Israel and pledged to give the matter high priority after taking office. At the same time, he repeated that the United States can have only one president speaking on its behalf at any given moment.

“Starting at the beginning of our administration, we are going to engage effectively and consistently to try to resolve the conflicts that exist in the Middle East,” Obama said.

CNN Senior International Correspondent Nic Robertson said the recording advances al-Zawahiri’s agenda in two respects: It attacks the incoming U.S. president before his inauguration and condemns Mubarak, whom al-Zawahiri has criticized for preventing supplies and humanitarian assistance from crossing Egypt’s border into Gaza.

Al-Zawahiri was born in Egypt and has previously been imprisoned there.

Reporting from the Israel-Gaza border on CNN’s “Situation Room,” Robertson also emphasized how rapidly the message was released. “Within 12 days, that’s very fast,” he said, adding that the quick response suggested the situation involved “many issues there that are dear to him.”

A purported audio message from al Qaeda’s deputy leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri, appeared on Islamist websites condemning Israel’s military offensive in the Gaza Strip and calling on Muslims around the world to rally against Israel. The recording’s authenticity could not be independently verified, but it bore the hallmarks of previous statements issued by al Qaeda’s media network.

In the message, al-Zawahiri accused Israel of committing atrocities against Palestinians and vowed that the offensive would not go unanswered. He urged Muslims to support the Palestinian cause and portrayed the fighting in Gaza as part of a broader struggle between Islam and Israel and its Western allies.

Al-Zawahiri also blamed the United States and regional governments for Palestinian suffering. He singled out Barack Obama, arguing that the incoming U.S. administration shared responsibility because of Washington’s continued support for Israel. Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak was also sharply criticized over Egypt’s policy toward Gaza and its control of the Rafah border crossing.

The statement reflected al Qaeda’s effort to exploit public anger over the conflict and present itself as a defender of Palestinians, despite the organization’s limited direct role in Gaza. It also sought to undermine Arab governments and challenge other Islamist movements by framing the crisis in terms of al Qaeda’s global militant ideology.

The recording emerged as Obama pledged to make Middle East peace a priority for his administration. The timing highlighted the difficulty facing U.S. and regional leaders as they sought to contain the Gaza conflict while militant groups attempted to use the violence to recruit supporters, intensify anti-Western sentiment and encourage further attacks against Israel and its allies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about Ayman al-Zawahiri’s audio message threatening revenge over Israel’s assault on Gaza and criticizing Barack Obama and Hosni Mubarak.
counterfactuals.output:
**Al Qaeda deputy threatens revenge over Gaza offensive**

**CAIRO, Egypt (CNN)** — Al Qaeda’s second-in-command, Ayman al-Zawahiri, threatened retaliation over Israel’s military offensive in Gaza and sharply criticized U.S. President Barack Obama and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in an audio message posted on Islamist websites.

The recording’s authenticity could not be independently verified. The voice appeared to resemble that of al-Zawahiri, an Egyptian-born physician who served as Osama bin Laden’s top deputy.

In the message, al-Zawahiri called on Muslims to respond to the Israeli operation and accused Arab governments of failing the Palestinians. He singled out Mubarak over Egypt’s restrictions at the Rafah border crossing with Gaza and portrayed Cairo as complicit in the blockade.

Al-Zawahiri also dismissed expectations that Obama’s presidency would bring a significant change in U.S. policy toward Israel and the Muslim world, accusing the new American administration of supporting Israeli actions.

The message appeared aimed at exploiting anger over Israel’s offensive against Hamas in Gaza, which caused extensive destruction and heavy Palestinian casualties. Israel said the operation was intended to stop rocket attacks from the Hamas-controlled territory.

U.S. and regional officials have long warned that al Qaeda uses conflicts involving Palestinians to recruit supporters, even though the group has no direct operational role in Gaza. Hamas and al Qaeda have also differed sharply in ideology and strategy.

There was no immediate response from the White House or the Egyptian government to the recording.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the January 2009 report about al Qaeda’s deputy leader responding to the Israel–Hamas fighting, including Obama’s reaction and Nic Robertson’s analysis.
counterfactuals.output:
A January 2009 report said al Qaeda deputy leader Ayman al-Zawahiri used an Internet audio message to portray Israel’s offensive against Hamas in Gaza as part of a broader Western “crusade” against Muslims. He condemned Israel, Arab governments, and President-elect Barack Obama, arguing that Obama’s support for Israeli security disproved his promise of change. Zawahiri urged Muslims to wage jihad and strike Israeli and Western interests.

Obama did not respond directly to Zawahiri. Addressing the Gaza war, he called the civilian deaths in Gaza and Israel a matter of “deep concern,” but repeated that the United States had only one president at a time and said he would speak and act more fully after his January 20 inauguration.

CNN’s Nic Robertson explained that al Qaeda was trying to exploit the powerful images and public anger from Gaza to regain relevance, recruit supporters, and inspire attacks. He noted, however, that al Qaeda and Hamas were not natural allies: Hamas is a Palestinian nationalist movement that participates in politics, while al Qaeda advocates a global jihad and has criticized Hamas. Thus, the message was less an endorsement of Hamas than an attempt to capitalize on the conflict.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a breaking-news article on the audio recording attributed to Ayman al-Zawahiri in which he urges militants to rally against Israel following the Gaza air strikes.
counterfactuals.output:
# Audio Attributed to Al-Zawahiri Urges Militants to Rally Against Israel After Gaza Strikes

**CAIRO — BREAKING:** An audio recording attributed to al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri has called on militants to rally against Israel following Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, according to a recording circulated through extremist media channels.

In the message, the speaker seeks to capitalize on anger over the Gaza violence, portraying the conflict as part of a broader regional struggle and urging armed groups to unite. The recording’s authenticity and date could not immediately be independently verified.

Al-Zawahiri, an Egyptian-born militant who became al-Qaeda’s leader after Osama bin Laden was killed in 2011, was himself killed in a U.S. drone strike in Kabul in July 2022. Any newly circulated recording attributed to him would therefore have been made before his death or could be previously released material resurfacing online.

Militant organizations have repeatedly used periods of heightened Israeli-Palestinian violence for propaganda and recruitment. Analysts caution that such statements do not necessarily indicate direct operational involvement in Gaza, where locally based Palestinian factions have historically dominated the armed confrontation with Israel.

Israeli officials did not immediately comment on the recording. Security agencies are expected to examine its origin, timing and whether it contains any evidence of a specific or credible threat.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recreate the CNN report covering al Qaeda’s vow of revenge for the Gaza offensive, preserving key quotations, background context, and commentary from CNN correspondent Nic Robertson.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t reproduce CNN’s report verbatim, but here is an original news-style reconstruction preserving its main points, brief quotations, and Nic Robertson’s analysis:

---

### Al Qaeda vows retaliation over Gaza offensive

Al Qaeda threatened revenge against Israel and its allies as anger spread across the Muslim world over Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

In a message distributed through jihadist media channels, senior al Qaeda figures portrayed the offensive as part of a wider war against Muslims and called for attacks on Israeli and Western interests. The group described the Gaza campaign as a “gift from Obama,” attempting to link the incoming U.S. administration to Washington’s longstanding support for Israel.

The statement came during Israel’s offensive against Hamas in Gaza, launched after continuing Palestinian rocket fire into southern Israel. The fighting caused extensive destruction and mounting civilian casualties, prompting demonstrations around the world and renewed demands for a cease-fire.

CNN correspondent Nic Robertson said al Qaeda was seeking to exploit outrage over the bloodshed. Rather than demonstrating that the organization had a direct role in the conflict, the threat showed its effort to absorb Gaza into its broader extremist narrative and use images of Palestinian suffering as a recruiting tool.

Robertson also noted that such declarations did not necessarily indicate an imminent operation. Al Qaeda had repeatedly used major conflicts involving Muslims to inspire supporters, encourage decentralized attacks, and present itself as the defender of Palestinians—even though the organization had little practical involvement in Gaza and ideological differences with Hamas.

The message nevertheless raised security concerns because it encouraged sympathizers to retaliate beyond the immediate conflict zone, potentially turning the Gaza offensive into a justification for attacks elsewhere.
